Thank you for submitting your article "A Model of Spatial Memory and Imagery – From Single Neurons to Cognition" for consideration by eLife. Your article has been reviewed by three peer reviewers, one of whom is a member of our Board of Reviewing Editors, and the evaluation has been overseen by Michael Frank as the Senior Editor. The reviewers have opted to remain anonymous.

The reviewers have discussed the reviews with one another and the Reviewing Editor has drafted this decision to help you prepare a revised submission.

Summary:

This paper describes a model that proposes a framework to explain how multiple, highly complex regions interact to produce egocentric and allocentric representations of space. Although all reviewers found the model to be interesting and novel, they also agreed that the Results, Materials and methods, and rationale for the model were often not presented in a clear and concise manner that would be optimal for a broad readership. Reviewers also felt that the simulation movies were insufficient to demonstrate the importance of the model and request a number of essential revisions, including incorporation of clear performance goals for the model, together with appropriate quantitative measures.

Essential revisions:

1) A primary shortcoming is that the model is not used to simulate any specific behavioral tasks. Instead, after describing the architecture, the paper presents a series of several simulations (depicted by figures and videos) to demonstrate examples of neural population activity (over time periods lasting tens of seconds) during a few selected types of navigational behavior. These example simulations do not provide adequate support for strong claims made in the Discussion section, where it is argued that the model accounts for a wide range of findings including position specificity in visual object memory (Hollingworth, 2007), impaired episodic memory resulting from Papez circuit lesions (Delay and Brion 1969), neural activity seen during imagery for scenes in the MTL, retrosplenial cortex and precuneus (Burgess, Maguire et al., 2001; Hassabis et al. 2007; Schacter et al. 2007), and 'some aspects' of 'scene construction' and 'episodic future thinking' (Schacter et al., 2007; Hassabis et al., 2007; Buckner 2010). To support such claims, the model should more faithfully reproduce experimental designs from these prior studies (as is, there does not seem to be any quantitative metric by which these broad claims can be evaluated). It is also implied that the model accounts for "trace cells" that fire when the agent visits the prior location of a missing object (Tsao et al., 2015), and although trace-like activity is shown in some example simulations, it is not specifically stated which neural population in the model would correspond to trace cells, nor are simulated trace cell firing rate maps presented. It is additionally claimed that the model accounts for preplay and replay activity of place cells, but it appears that simulated preplay and replay events do not occur on a compressed time scale in the model as they do in real rodents, which is not addressed. In other words, the heavy reliance on qualitative (rather than quantitative) performance assessments make it difficult to offer anything more than a subjective evaluation of the model's capabilities. A more objective evaluation might be possible if the authors run more simulations to quantitatively compare simulated vs. real neural activity (or simulated vs. real task performance), explore how the model's performance degrades under realistic noise or uncertainty conditions, etc.

2) Several key mechanisms – such as sequential shifting of attentional focus (which is essential for solving the place-object binding problem), neuromodulation (which allows the model to transition between sensory processing and mental imagery modes), and population activity in the grid cell map (which is essential for generating preplay/replay trajectories) – are not explicitly simulated by the model. Rather, these signals are provided "for free" as inputs to the network. When reciting the list of phenomena that the model can explain (see prior point), the authors should take care to include only phenomena that fall within the purview of what is actually being simulated by the network, rather what is being provided for free.

3) The depiction and explanation of BVC and PWb data (initially shown in Figure 2A2, C1, and C2 and also described in subsequent figures) is unclear. Why are small receptive fields shown close to the agent in Figure 2A2? What does this mean? In the Video 1, receptive fields do not appear to get smaller or bigger as the agent moves around. Are the cells with receptive fields close to the agent the ones that fire at the actual boundaries, not a distance away from the boundaries? If not, in Figure 2C1, why are BVCs shown to be firing, presumably at the north and east boundaries of the environment, when the agent is in the center of the environment (i.e., not in the boundary)? Why are so many BVCs firing at the same time when the agent is in a particular location? Are these different cells that fire at different distances from the boundaries? Figure 2A2 is described as showing receptive fields for BVCs, but these receptive fields are usually more rectangular in shape, whereas they are depicted as circular here. In "bottom up" mode (e.g., Figure 5, top) it appears that only BVCs encoding boundaries ahead of the animal (those in the visual field?) are active. Is this consistent with the firing of real neurons (such as border cells)? Is there any evidence that real BVCs are active only when a rodent faces toward but not away from their coded boundary?

4) The authors show a schematic of their model in Figure 4, which includes top-down and bottom-up connections between different brain areas. Lacking from the paper are multiple citations to anatomical studies that demonstrate that these connections are realistic (e.g., Jones and Witter, 2007, for projections from retrosplenial cortex to deep layers of entorhinal cortex). For example, has it been shown that the entorhinal cortex projects back to the retrosplenial cortex?

5) In Figure 7D, why isn't anything activated for the new object?

6) The authors go to great lengths to realistically model MTL activity based on rodent literature. However, it was not clear how the model relates to rodent literature regarding parietal coding (e.g. Harvey, Coen and Tank, 2012; Raposo, Kaufman and Churchland, 2014; Whitlock et al., 2012) and retrosplenial coding (Vedder, Miller, Harrison, Smith, Cerebral Cortex, 2017; Alexander and Nitz, 2017; Alexander and Nitz, 2015). Can the model account for the type of coding observed in navigating rodents in these regions? Or are there specific predictions the model can make about what would be observed or how these types of observed neural codes can be interpreted in the context of spatial cognition?

7) In some places, terms are used that assume prior knowledge to a degree that can make the paper difficult to parse. Some examples include 'gain-field circuit' (Introduction), the current model as an extension of the 'BBB model' (Introduction), 'heuristically implemented', 'mock-motor-efference'. Terms like this could use additional (but very brief) explanation when introduced.

8) The paper can be a bit long in places – particularly the sections on preplay and replay.

9) Figure 4: was activity from place cells to grid cells considered?

10) The presence of object specific coding appears to be a 'strong prediction' of the model, as object coding reported thus far is minimally selective for specific objects. The authors detail potential places where this activity might be found but they may want to consider that these types of representations lay outside the cortex or emerge as a population level representation (i.e. would not be observable at the level of single cell tuning curve responses).

Thank you for submitting your work entitled "A Neural-Level Model of Spatial Memory and Imagery" for consideration by eLife. Your article has been reviewed by one peer reviewer, and the evaluation has been overseen by a Reviewing Editor and a Senior Editor. The reviewers have opted to remain anonymous.

We regret to inform you that your work will not be considered further for publication in eLife.

After consultation, we feel that the paper remains too cumbersome for a general audience, and some points remain unclear.

Reviewer #3:

In this paper, Bicanski and Burgess present a network model to propose how multiple populations of spatially tuned neurons are functionally interconnected with one another to form a spatial memory network with multiple capabilities.

A core feature of the model is that it proposes how bidirectional transformations between the egocentric and allocentric reference frames might be performed by networks in the retrosplenial cortex. The paper ambitiously attempts to demonstrate numerous capabilities for the model, such as mapping a familiar environment, learning the locations of unique landmark objects in such an environment, detecting novelty when changes occur in an environment, and simulating effects of brain lesions upon memory and navigation. The paper incorporates 13 videos, 13 figures, and 18 methods equations. Despite its length (nearly 60 pages), the paper does not provide enough detail for readers to fully understand some key aspects of the model (see below). This should not be interpreted as an entreaty to make the paper even longer. Rather, the paper should probably be split up into at least two publications, each dedicated to exploring specific capabilities of the model with more clarity and depth.

As noted in the prior review, simulations of mental navigation and route planning do not seem to be rooted in the model's core ability to perform bidirectional egocentric / allocentric transformations. Instead, it is the addition ("for free") of a grid cell network connected to place cells endows the model with this capability. How does the egocentric / allocentric transformation network contribute to the mental navigation and route-planning process? What is the functional purpose for transforming allocentric replay events back into the egocentric coordinate frame to generate imagery? The grid cell driven simulations do not even appear until the subsection “Grid cells and mental navigation (Simulation 4.0)”, and given how information dense the preceding pages are, perhaps the addition of the grid cell network and accompanying simulations might be better suited to a second paper, dedicated more specifically to the topic of route planning?

Another problem raised in review, which has not been adequately addressed, is that the sequential shifting of attentional focus is not explicitly simulated by the model, and not explained fully enough for readers to comprehend how this process contributes to the simulation results. To solve the problem of binding each object or boundary's location to its identity, the model adopts a sequential shift of attention strategy. If I understand correctly, each population of boundary (BVC) or object (OVC) cells is activated one at a time in conjunction with its corresponding boundary (PRb) or object (PRo) identity cell. The length of each attentional cycle is stated to be 600 time units. How does information about multiple objects and boundaries get integrated across multiple attentional cycles to form a stable and non-fluctuating representation of the environment as a whole? Do PCs have slow activity decay kinetics that can span multiple attentional cycles? How is such temporal integration accounted for in analyses like that shown in Figure 8, where momentary "snapshots" of population vectors are being correlated with one another across encoding vs. recall? Because of the sequential attention mechanism, one would expect that an incomplete representation of the environment (i.e., just one object and one boundary) would be active at any given time. So I don't quite see how it is possible to use an instantaneous snapshot of the population vector to perform these correlation analyses, unless the snapshot is being taken at the end of some temporal integration process that spans multiple attention cycles?

Finally, since the heart of the model is the retrosplenial transformation network, it is a bit surprising that no simulation results are shown to demonstrate the predicted firing properties of retrosplenial neurons that perform the egocentric / allocentric transformation (in either direction) during imagery and recall. Do any testable predictions for unit recording studies arise from the firing properties of these model neurons? If so, then it seems like they should be included in the paper.

In summary, there are some innovative features of this model that would of interest to the research community, but the format of the paper (including its length) may not be best suited for publication in eLife. The authors might wish to consider splitting the paper up into two publications (e.g., one on coordinate transformation, and one on mental navigation and route following) so that some of the missing details of the model can be more thoroughly described without adding even more to the current manuscript's excessive length.

Thank you for resubmitting your work entitled "A Neural-Level Model of Spatial Memory and Imagery" for further consideration at eLife. Your revised article has been favorably evaluated by Michael Frank (Senior Editor), a Reviewing Editor, and one new reviewer.

The manuscript has been improved but there are some remaining issues that need to be addressed before acceptance, as outlined below:

Reviewer #1:

In the revised manuscript, the authors have done a lot of work to respond to previous criticisms, including adding new results to respond to the initial criticisms.

There is much value and novelty in this model, which provides a potential explanation of how egocentric and allocentric representations of space are reconciled. Also, as the authors point out in their appeal, the excessive length of the manuscript is due to results that were added to satisfy the original reviews. I feel confident that the specific feedback provided below will allow the authors to clarify points that remain puzzling.

1) I didn't really understand what the "transformation sublayers" are. Are they between areas or in the retrosplenial cortex part of the model? How are they different from "individual sublayers" (subsection “The Head Direction Attractor Network and the Transformation Circuit”, second paragraph)?

2) In all of the figures and videos involving the top-down mode/recall/imagery, why does firing occur for all directions of boundaries in PWbs and BVCs?

claims.source: That this transformation between egocentric directions (left, right, ahead) and environmentally-referenced directions (nominally North, South, East, West) requires input from the head-direction cells found along Papez's circuit (Taube et al., 1990a; Taube et al., 1990b) is consistent with its involvement in episodic memory (e.g. Aggleton and Brown, 1999; Delay and Brion, 1969).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Taube et al., 1990a; Taube et al., 1990b; Aggleton and Brown, 1999; Delay and Brion, 1969.

claims.claim: During perception the egocentric parietal window representation is based on sensory inputs and driven in a bottom-up manner.
claims.source: During perception the egocentric parietal window representation is based on (highly processed) sensory inputs. That is, it is driven in a bottom-up manner, and the transformation circuit maps the egocentric PWb representation to allocentric BVCs.
claims.evidence: This describes the bottom-up mode of operation in the model.

claims.claim: When the transformation circuit acts in reverse (top-down mode), it reconstructs the parietal representation from BVCs.
claims.source: When the transformation circuit acts in reverse (top-down mode), it reconstructs the parietal representation from BVCs which are co-active with other medial temporal cell populations, forming the substrate of viewpoint-independent (i.e. allocentric) memory.
claims.evidence: This describes the top-down mode of operation in the model.

claims.claim: The reverse transformation yields an orientation-specific egocentric parietal representation and constitutes the model's account of spatial imagery and explicit recall.
claims.source: This yields an orientation-specific (egocentric) parietal representation (a specific point of view) and constitutes the model's account of (spatial) imagery and explicit recall of spatial configurations of known spaces (Burgess et al., 2001a; Byrne et al., 2007).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Burgess et al., 2001a; Byrne et al., 2007.

claims.claim: The model proposes allocentric object vector cells (OVCs) analogous to BVCs.
claims.source: To account for the presence of objects within the environment, we propose allocentric object vector cells (OVCs) analogous to BVCs, and show how object-locations can be embedded into spatial memory, supported by visuo-spatial attention.
claims.evidence: This is a novel prediction of the model.

claims.claim: The proposed object-coding populations in the MTL map onto recently discovered neuronal populations.
claims.source: Importantly, the proposed object-coding populations in the MTL map onto recently discovered neuronal populations (Deshmukh and Knierim, 2013; Hoydal et al., 2017).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Deshmukh and Knierim, 2013; Hoydal et al., 2017.

claims.claim: The model predicts a population of egocentric object-coding cells in the parietal window (PWo cells).
claims.source: We also predict a population of egocentric object-coding cells in the parietal window (PWo cells: egocentric analogues to OVCs), as well as directionally modulated boundary and object coding neurons (in the transformation circuit).
claims.evidence: This is a novel prediction of the model.

claims.claim: The model predicts directionally modulated boundary and object coding neurons in the transformation circuit.
claims.source: We also predict a population of egocentric object-coding cells in the parietal window (PWo cells: egocentric analogues to OVCs), as well as directionally modulated boundary and object coding neurons (in the transformation circuit).
claims.evidence: This is a novel prediction of the model.

claims.claim: The model includes a grid cell population to account for mental navigation and planning.
claims.source: Finally, we include a grid cell population to account for mental navigation and planning, which drives sequential place cell firing reminiscent of hippocampal 'replay' (Wilson and McNaughton, 1994; Foster and Wilson, 2006; Diba and Buzsáki, 2007; Karlsson and Frank, 2009; Carr et al., 2011) and preplay (Dragoi and Tonegawa, 2011; Ólafsdóttir et al., 2015).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Wilson and McNaughton, 1994; Foster and Wilson, 2006; Diba and Buzsáki, 2007; Karlsson and Frank, 2009; Carr et al., 2011; Dragoi and Tonegawa, 2011; Ólafsdóttir et al., 2015.

claims.claim: Cells that encode an egocentric representation of boundary locations have recently been described.
claims.source: Intriguingly, cells that encode an egocentric representation of boundary locations (akin to parietal window neurons in the present model) have recently been described (Hinman et al., 2017).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by citation to Hinman et al., 2017.

claims.claim: Head direction cells are arranged in a simple ring-attractor circuit.
claims.source: Head direction cells (HDCs) are arranged in a simple ring-attractor circuit (Skaggs et al., 1995; Zhang, 1996).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Skaggs et al., 1995; Zhang, 1996.

claims.claim: Current head direction is updated by angular velocity information as the agent explores the environment.
claims.source: Current head direction, encoded by activity in this attractor circuit, is updated by angular velocity information as the agent explores the environment.
claims.evidence: This describes how the head direction system operates in the model.

claims.claim: The retrosplenial transformation circuit consists of 20 sublayers.
claims.source: The retrosplenial transformation circuit (RSC/TR) consists of 20 sublayers.
claims.evidence: This is a specific architectural detail of the model.

claims.claim: Each sublayer of the transformation circuit is a copy of the BVC population, with firing tuned to a specific head-direction.
claims.source: Each sublayer is a copy of the BVC population, with firing within each sublayer also tuned to a specific head-direction (directions are evenly spaced in the [0360] degree range).
claims.evidence: This is a specific architectural detail of the model.

claims.claim: Individual cells in the transformation circuit are directionally modulated boundary vector cells.
claims.source: That is, individual cells in the transformation circuit are directionally modulated boundary vector cells, and connect egocentric (parietal) PWb neurons and allocentric BVCs (in the MTL) in a mutually consistent way.
claims.evidence: This is a specific architectural detail of the model.

claims.claim: All connections in the transformation circuit are reciprocal.
claims.source: All connections are reciprocal.
claims.evidence: This is a specific architectural detail of the model.

claims.claim: The balance between bottom-up and top-down connections is subject to neuromodulation.
claims.source: To implement the switch between modes of operation, we assume that the balance between bottom-up and top-down connections is subject to neuromodulation (see e.g. Hasselmo, 2006); Appendix, Equation 3 and following).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by citation to Hasselmo, 2006.

claims.claim: Connections from the parietal window to the transformation circuit are at full strength in bottom-up mode but down-regulated to 5% in top-down mode.
claims.source: For example, connections from the parietal window (PWb and PWo) populations to the transformation circuit and thence onto BVCs/OVCs are at full strength in bottom-up mode, but down-regulated to 5% of their maximum value in top-down mode.
claims.evidence: This is a specific implementation detail of the model.

claims.claim: Connections from BVCs/OVCs to the transformation circuit are down-regulated during bottom-up perception and reach full strength during imagery.
claims.source: Conversely, connections from BVCs/OVCs to the transformation circuit and onwards to the parietal window are down-regulated during bottom-up perception (5% of their maximum value) and reach full strength only during imagery (top-down reconstruction).
claims.evidence: This is a specific implementation detail of the model.

claims.claim: To uniquely characterize the egocentric perceptual state of encountering an object requires co-activation of perirhinal neurons and the corresponding parietal window.
claims.source: As noted above (section "The Role of Perirhinal Neurons"), to uniquely characterize the egocentric perceptual state of encountering an object within an environment requires the co-activation of perirhinal (PRo) neurons (signaling identity) and the corresponding parietal window (PWo) (signaling location in peripersonal space).
claims.evidence: This is a theoretical claim about the requirements for object representation.

claims.claim: Maximal co-firing of only one PRo neuron with one PWo neuron at a given location is required for an unambiguous association.
claims.source: Moreover, maximal co-firing of only one PRo neuron with one PWo neuron (or OVC, in allocentric terms) at a given location is required for an unambiguous association (Figure 3A–C).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by reference to Figure 3A-C.

claims.claim: The agent directs attention to each visible object in sequence to ensure a unique representation.
claims.source: To ensure a unique representation, we allow the agent to direct attention to each visible object in sequence (compare Figure 3B and C; for a review of attentional mechanisms see VanRullen, 2013).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by reference to Figure 3B and C and citation to VanRullen, 2013.

claims.claim: A fixed length for an attentional cycle is set at 600 time units.
claims.source: We set a fixed length for an attentional cycle (600 time units).
claims.evidence: This is a specific implementation detail of the model.

claims.claim: Grid cell firing is thought to update the location represented by place cell firing, driven by signals relating to self-motion.
claims.source: Grid cell (GC) firing is thought to update the location represented by place cell firing, driven by signals relating to self-motion (O'Keefe and Burgess, 2005; McNaughton et al., 2006; Fuhs and Touretzky, 2006; Solstad et al., 2006).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by citations to O'Keefe and Burgess, 2005; McNaughton et al., 2006; Fuhs and Touretzky, 2006; Solstad et al., 2006.

claims.claim: During imagination, grid cell firing is driven by mock motor-efference signals and used to translate the activity bump on the sheet of place cells.
claims.source: During imagination, we suppose that GC firing is driven by mock motor-efference signals (i.e. imagined movement without actual motor output) and used to translate the activity bump on the sheet of place cells.
claims.evidence: This is a theoretical claim about how grid cells support imagery.

claims.claim: Both self-motion inputs via grid cells and sensory inputs converge onto place cells and may be weighted according to their reliability.
claims.source: Importantly, both self-motion inputs (via GCs) and sensory inputs (e.g. mediated via BVCs and OVCs) converge onto PCs and both types of inputs may be weighted according to their reliability (Evans et al., 2016).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by citation to Evans et al., 2016.

claims.claim: Grid cells could support place cell activity when sensory inputs are unreliable or absent.
claims.source: GCs could thus support PC activity when sensory inputs are unreliable or absent.
claims.evidence: This is a theoretical claim about the role of grid cells.

claims.claim: Connection weights between grid cells and place cells are calculated as a simple Hebbian association.
claims.source: Connection weights between GCs and PCs are calculated as a simple Hebbian association between PC firing at a given coordinate (according to the mapping shown in Figure 2A,B) and pre-calculated firing rate maps of GCs (7 modules with 100 cells each, see Appendix for details).
claims.evidence: This is a specific implementation detail of the model, with reference to Figure 2A,B.

claims.claim: Recollection in the BB-model results in visuo-spatial imagery of a coherent scene from a single viewpoint and direction.
claims.source: Recollection in the BB-model results in visuo-spatial imagery of a coherent scene from a single viewpoint and direction, that is it implements a process of scene construction (Burgess et al., 2001a; Byrne et al., 2007; Schacter et al., 2007; Hassabis et al., 2007; Buckner, 2010) at the neuronal level.
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Burgess et al., 2001a; Byrne et al., 2007; Schacter et al., 2007; Hassabis et al., 2007; Buckner, 2010.

claims.claim: Similar tasks in humans appear to engage the full network, including Papez' circuit, retrosplenial cortex, medial parietal areas, parahippocampus and hippocampus, and possibly the entorhinal cortex.
claims.source: Similar tasks in humans appear to engage the full network, including Papez' circuit, where head direction cells are found (for review see Taube, 2007); retrosplenial cortex (where we hypothesize the transformation circuit to be located) (Burgess et al., 2001a; Lambrey et al., 2012; Auger and Maguire, 2013; Epstein and Vass, 2014; Marchette et al., 2014; Shine et al., 2016); medial parietal areas (Fletcher et al., 1996; Hebscher et al., 2018); parahippocampus and hippocampus (Hassabis et al., 2007; Addis et al., 2007; Schacter et al., 2007; Bird et al., 2010); and possibly the entorhinal cortex (Atance and O'Neill, 2001; Bellmund et al., 2016; Horner et al. 2016; also see Simulation 4.0).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by multiple citations including Taube, 2007; Burgess et al., 2001a; Lambrey et al., 2012; Auger and Maguire, 2013; Epstein and Vass, 2014; Marchette et al., 2014; Shine et al., 2016; Fletcher et al., 1996; Hebscher et al., 2018; Hassabis et al., 2007; Addis et al., 2007; Schacter et al., 2007; Bird et al., 2010; Atance and O'Neill, 2001; Bellmund et al., 2016; Horner et al. 2016.

claims.claim: BVCs were predicted by an early predecessor of the present model.
claims.source: Notably, BVCs were predicted by an early predecessor of the present model (Hartley et al., 2000; Burgess et al., 2001a).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Hartley et al., 2000; Burgess et al., 2001a.

claims.claim: OVC-like responses have been reported recently.
claims.source: Intriguingly, OVC-like responses have been reported recently (Deshmukh and Knierim, 2013; Hoydal et al., 2017).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Deshmukh and Knierim, 2013; Hoydal et al., 2017.

claims.claim: Anatomical connections between the potential loci of BVCs/OVCs and retrosplenial cortex exist.
claims.source: Anatomical connections between the potential loci of BVCs/OVCs and retrosplenial cortex (the suggested location of the egocentric-allocentric transformation circuit) exist. BVCs have been found in the subicular complex (Lever et al., 2009), and the related border cells and OVCs in medial entorhinal cortex (Solstad et al., 2008; Hoydal et al., 2017). Both areas receive projections from retrosplenial cortex (Jones and Witter, 2007), and project back to it (Wyss and Van Groen, 1992).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Lever et al., 2009; Solstad et al., 2008; Hoydal et al., 2017; Jones and Witter, 2007; Wyss and Van Groen, 1992.

claims.claim: Lesions along Papez' circuit have long been known to induce amnesia.
claims.source: Lesions along Papez' circuit have long been known to induce amnesia (Delay and Brion, 1969; Squire and Slater, 1978; 1989; Parker and Gaffan, 1997; Aggleton et al., 2016).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Delay and Brion, 1969; Squire and Slater, 1978; 1989; Parker and Gaffan, 1997; Aggleton et al., 2016.

claims.claim: Lesions to the fornix and mammilary bodies severely impact recollection, although recognition can be less affected.
claims.source: Thus, lesions to the fornix and mammilary bodies severely impact recollection, although recognition can be less affected (Tsivilis et al., 2008).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by citation to Tsivilis et al., 2008.

claims.claim: The mammillary bodies, anterior dorsal thalamus, retrosplenial cortex, parts of the subicular complex and medial entorhinal cortex all contain head direction cells.
claims.source: That is, the mammillary bodies (more specifically the lateral mammillary nucleus, LMN), anterior dorsal thalamus, retrosplenial cortex, parts of the subicular complex and medial entorhinal cortex all contain head direction cells (Taube, 2007; Sargolini et al., 2006).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Taube, 2007; Sargolini et al., 2006.

claims.claim: In the bottom-up mode of operation, a lesion removes drive to the transformation circuit and consequently to the boundary vector cells and object vector cells.
claims.source: In the bottom-up mode of operation (perception), the lesion removes drive to the transformation circuit and consequently to the boundary vector cells and object vector cells.
claims.evidence: This describes the effect of a simulated lesion in the model.

claims.claim: A lesion to Papez' circuit causes the perceived location of an object to be unable to elicit activity in the MTL and thus cannot be encoded into memory.
claims.source: That is, the perceived location of an object (present in the egocentric parietal representation) cannot elicit activity in the MTL and thus cannot be encoded into memory (Figure 7).
claims.evidence: This describes the effect of a simulated lesion in the model, with reference to Figure 7.

claims.claim: The model is robust to adding firing rate noise up to 20% of peak firing rate to all cells.
claims.source: The model is also robust to adding firing rate noise (up to 20% of peak firing rate) to all cells. Correlations between patterns at encoding and recall remain similar to the noise-free case, see Figure 8C.
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by simulation results shown in Figure 8C.

claims.claim: Rats show a spontaneous preference for exploring novel/altered stimuli compared to familiar/unchanged ones.
claims.source: Rats show a spontaneous preference for exploring novel/altered stimuli compared to familiar/unchanged ones.
claims.evidence: This is a well-known behavioral phenomenon in rodents.

claims.claim: Rats preferentially explore one of two objects that has been shifted to a new location within a given environment, a behavior impaired by hippocampal lesions.
claims.source: We simulate one of these experiments (Mumby et al., 2002), in which rats preferentially explore one of two objects that has been shifted to a new location within a given environment, a behavior impaired by hippocampal lesions.
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by citation to Mumby et al., 2002.

claims.claim: With an intact hippocampus, the moved object generates a significant novelty signal due to the mismatch between recalled and perceptual OVC firing.
claims.source: With an intact hippocampus (Figure 9; Video 7), the moved object generates a significant novelty signal, due to the mismatch between recalled (top-down) OVC firing and perceptual (bottom-up) OVC firing at the encoding location.
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by simulation results shown in Figure 9 and Video 7.

claims.claim: Detection of a change in object position requires the hippocampus.
claims.source: That detection of a change in position requires the hippocampus is consistent with place cells binding the relative location of an object (via object vector cells) to perirhinal neurons signalling the identity of an object.
claims.evidence: This is a theoretical claim about the role of the hippocampus.

claims.claim: Rats show preferential exploration of a familiar object that was previously experienced in a different environment compared with one previously experienced in the same environment.
claims.source: Rats also show preferential exploration of a familiar object that was previously experienced in a different environment, compared with one previously experienced in the same environment, and this preference is also abolished by hippocampal lesions (Mumby et al., 2002; Eacott and Norman, 2004; Langston and Wood, 2010).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Mumby et al., 2002; Eacott and Norman, 2004; Langston and Wood, 2010.

claims.claim: Object recognition irrespective of context is spared after hippocampal but not perirhinal lesions.
claims.source: Finally, it has been argued that object recognition (irrespective of context) is spared after hippocampal but not perirhinal lesions (Aggleton and Brown, 1999; Winters et al., 2004; Norman and Eacott, 2004) which would be compatible with the model given that its perirhinal neuronal population signals an object's identity irrespective of location.
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Aggleton and Brown, 1999; Winters et al., 2004; Norman and Eacott, 2004.

claims.claim: In rodents, it has been proposed that encoding and retrieval are gated by the theta rhythm.
claims.source: In rodents, it has been proposed that encoding and retrieval are gated by the theta rhythm (Hasselmo et al., 2002): a constantly present modulation of the local field potential during exploration.
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by citation to Hasselmo et al., 2002.

claims.claim: In humans, theta is restricted to shorter bursts, but is associated with encoding and retrieval.
claims.source: In humans, theta is restricted to shorter bursts, but is associated with encoding and retrieval (Düzel et al., 2010).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by citation to Düzel et al., 2010.

claims.claim: Trace cells in lateral entorhinal cortex reflect the previous presence of a now missing object.
claims.source: Interestingly, Tsao et al. (2013) recently reported 'trace cells' in lateral entorhinal cortex, whose firing reflects the previous presence of a now missing object, while related 'mis-place' cells have been reported in CA1 (O'Keefe, 1976).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Tsao et al. (2013) and O'Keefe, 1976.

claims.claim: Nominally non-spatially selective cells like perirhinal identity neurons can manifest a spatial trace firing field when re-activation occurs at the encoding location.
claims.source: We have shown that nominally non-spatially selective cells like perirhinal identity neurons can manifest a spatial trace firing field when re-activation occurs at the encoding location (Figure 10D3).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by simulation results shown in Figure 10D3.

claims.claim: Humans can focus attention on different elements in an imagined scene, sampling one after another, without necessarily adopting a new imagined viewpoint.
claims.source: Humans can focus attention on different elements in an imagined scene, sampling one after another, without necessarily adopting a new imagined viewpoint.
claims.evidence: This is a well-known cognitive capability.

claims.claim: Humans can localize an object in imagined scenes and retrieve its identity.
claims.source: Moreover, humans can localize an object in imagined scenes and retrieve its identity (e.g. 'What was next to the fireplace in the restaurant we ate at?").
claims.evidence: This is a well-known cognitive capability.

claims.claim: Grid cell firing is thought to update the location represented by place cell firing, driven by signals relating to self-motion.
claims.source: Grid cell (GC) firing is thought to update the location represented by place cell firing, driven by signals relating to self-motion (O'Keefe and Burgess, 2005; McNaughton et al., 2006; Fuhs and Touretzky, 2006; Solstad et al., 2006).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by citations to O'Keefe and Burgess, 2005; McNaughton et al., 2006; Fuhs and Touretzky, 2006; Solstad et al., 2006.

claims.claim: Humans likely make use of spatial imagery even in apparently non-visual tasks such as triangle completion in darkness.
claims.source: Indeed, humans likely make use of spatial imagery even in apparently non-visual tasks such as triangle completion in darkness (Tcheang et al., 2011), and there is evidence for grid-like brain activity during mental navigation (Bellmund et al., 2016; Horner et al. 2016).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Tcheang et al., 2011; Bellmund et al., 2016; Horner et al. 2016.

claims.claim: Grid cells have been proposed to support the computation of vectors to a goal.
claims.source: Grid cells have been proposed to support the computation of vectors to a goal (Kubie and Fenton, 2012; Erdem and Hasselmo, 2012; Bush et al., 2015; Stemmler et al., 2015).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Kubie and Fenton, 2012; Erdem and Hasselmo, 2012; Bush et al., 2015; Stemmler et al., 2015.

claims.claim: The model proposes that grid cells recruit new hippocampal cells (future place cells) in previously unexplored parts of a familiar environment.
claims.source: We proposed that grid cells recruit new hippocampal cells (future place cells) in previously unexplored parts of a familiar environment (Figure 13 and Video 13).
claims.evidence: This is a theoretical claim of the model, with reference to Figure 13 and Video 13.

claims.claim: Planning a trajectory across unexplored space engenders preplay-like activity in place cells.
claims.source: Planning a trajectory across unexplored space engenders preplay-like activity in place cells (Dragoi and Tonegawa, 2011; Ólafsdóttir et al., 2015), whereas mental navigation is reminiscent of 'replay' (Wilson and McNaughton, 1994; Foster and Wilson, 2006; Diba and Buzsáki, 2007; Karlsson and Frank, 2009; Carr et al., 2011) or 'forward sweeps (Johnson and Redish, 2007; Pfeiffer and Foster, 2015), although the faster propagation speed (e.g. during sharp wave ripples) of these sequences of place cell activity are beyond the scope of the present model.
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Dragoi and Tonegawa, 2011; Ólafsdóttir et al., 2015; Wilson and McNaughton, 1994; Foster and Wilson, 2006; Diba and Buzsáki, 2007; Karlsson and Frank, 2009; Carr et al., 2011; Johnson and Redish, 2007; Pfeiffer and Foster, 2015.

claims.claim: It has been argued that the MTL-retrosplenial-parietal system supports the construction of coherent scenes.
claims.source: It has been argued that the MTL-retrosplenial-parietal system supports the construction of coherent scenes (Burgess et al., 2001b; Byrne et al., 2007; Hassabis et al., 2007; Schacter et al., 2007; Buckner, 2010).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Burgess et al., 2001b; Byrne et al., 2007; Hassabis et al., 2007; Schacter et al., 2007; Buckner, 2010.

claims.claim: If recollection corresponds to the reconstruction of something akin to a perceptual experience, then this places strong spatial constraints on how episodic memory works.
claims.source: However, if recollection corresponds to the (re-)construction of something akin to a perceptual experience (the defining characteristic of episodic memory; Tulving 1985), then this places strong spatial constraints on how episodic memory works.
claims.evidence: This is a theoretical claim supported by citation to Tulving 1985.

claims.claim: Only a small subset of information combinations would be consistent with a single point of view, making episodic re-experiencing congruent with perceptual experiences.
claims.source: A vast number of different combinations of information could be retrieved from the body of long-term knowledge in the MTL, but only a small subset would be consistent with a single point of view, making the episodic 're-experiencing' of events or visuo-spatial imagery congruent with perceptual experiences.
claims.evidence: This is a theoretical claim about the constraints on episodic memory.

claims.claim: The model distinguishes the egocentric representations supporting conscious re-experience from the more abstract allocentric representations involved in supporting computations.
claims.source: This account includes functional roles for the specific firing characteristics of diverse populations of spatially selective cells across multiple brain regions, and distinguishes the egocentric representations supporting conscious (re-)experience from the more abstract (allocentric) representations involved in supporting computations.
claims.evidence: This is a core theoretical claim of the model.

claims.claim: The model follows Tulving's theoretical specification of episodic memory.
claims.source: It follows Tulving's theoretical specification of episodic memory, and - spanning Marr's theoretical, algorithmic and implementational levels (Marr and Poggio, 1976) - bridges the gap between a neuropsychological description of spatial cognition (founded on behavioral and functional imaging data) and the neural representations supporting it.
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by citation to Marr and Poggio, 1976.

claims.claim: The model spans Marr's theoretical, algorithmic and implementational levels.
claims.source: It follows Tulving's theoretical specification of episodic memory, and - spanning Marr's theoretical, algorithmic and implementational levels (Marr and Poggio, 1976) - bridges the gap between a neuropsychological description of spatial cognition (founded on behavioral and functional imaging data) and the neural representations supporting it.
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by citation to Marr and Poggio, 1976.

claims.claim: The model bridges the gap between a neuropsychological description of spatial cognition and the neural representations supporting it.
claims.source: It follows Tulving's theoretical specification of episodic memory, and - spanning Marr's theoretical, algorithmic and implementational levels (Marr and Poggio, 1976) - bridges the gap between a neuropsychological description of spatial cognition (founded on behavioral and functional imaging data) and the neural representations supporting it.
claims.evidence: This is a core claim about the contribution of the model.

claims.claim: Object memory is superior when the target object is presented at the same position in the scene as it had been viewed originally.
claims.source: Attaching representations of discrete objects (in the form of object vector cell activity) to a contextual representation via place cells aligns well with neuropsychological experiments that show position specificity in visual object memory (Hollingworth, 2007). In such experiments, object memory is superior when the target object is presented at the same position in the scene as it had been viewed originally (also see object novelty Simulations 1.3, 1.4).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by citation to Hollingworth, 2007.

claims.claim: The hippocampus in particular has been implicated in combining information about objects, locations, and contexts.
claims.source: The hippocampus in particular has been implicated in combining information about objects, locations, and contexts (Warburton and Brown, 2010; Eacott and Gaffan, 2005; Barker and Warburton, 2015), consistent with the model.
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Warburton and Brown, 2010; Eacott and Gaffan, 2005; Barker and Warburton, 2015.

claims.claim: Studies suggest the hippocampus and precuneus are necessary for maintaining object-location binding even in working memory.
claims.source: Similarly, studies suggest the hippocampus and precuneus are necessary for maintaining object-location binding even in working memory (Piekema et al., 2006; Olson et al., 2006).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Piekema et al., 2006; Olson et al., 2006.

claims.claim: The direction-independence of place cell firing in open environments implies that all possible local views at a given location could be associated with the corresponding place cells.
claims.source: The direction-independence of place cell firing in open environments implies that all possible local views at a given location could be associated with the corresponding place cells, potentially encompassing the boundaries in all directions around that location.
claims.evidence: This is a theoretical claim based on known properties of place cells.

claims.claim: Permanent landmarks should evoke stronger responses in retrosplenial cortex because they provide a more stable directional reference for the transformation circuit.
claims.source: It also explains why permanent landmarks should evoke stronger responses in retrosplenial cortex (Auger et al., 2012), because permanent landmarks provide a more stable directional reference for the transformation circuit (see also Bicanski and Burgess, 2016).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Auger et al., 2012 and Bicanski and Burgess, 2016.

claims.claim: Head direction cells likely serve to specify a direction of view, and not a movement direction.
claims.source: In summary, head direction cells likely serve to specify a direction of view, and not a movement direction (Raudies et al., 2015), which could instead be expressed in the firing phase of grid cells or place cells (Maurer et al., 2014; Cei et al., 2014).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Raudies et al., 2015; Maurer et al., 2014; Cei et al., 2014.

claims.claim: The encoding strategy for objects allows an agent to reactivate the set of place cells which were active when the object was encountered.
claims.source: The encoding strategy for objects allows an agent to reactivate the set of place cells which were active when the object was encountered and thus reconstruct the local view at encoding in the parietal window.
claims.evidence: This is a theoretical claim about how the model supports recall.

claims.claim: The model provides an explanation for the neural activity seen in the MTL, retrosplenial cortex and precuneus during imagery for familiar scenes.
claims.source: This models the explicit recollection of a spatial scene populated with objects as an act of visuo-spatial imagery. It provides an explanation for the neural activity seen in the MTL, retrosplenial cortex and precuneus during imagery for familiar scenes (Burgess et al., 2001a; Hassabis et al., 2007; Schacter et al., 2007).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Burgess et al., 2001a; Hassabis et al., 2007; Schacter et al., 2007.

claims.claim: The agent could use the place cells activated during imagery as 'goal cells' and use grid cells to calculate a vector to navigate to the remembered location.
claims.source: The agent could also use the place cells activated during imagery as 'goal cells' and use grid cells to calculate a vector to navigate to the remembered location (Bush et al., 2015); not simulated here), accounting for the role of the MTL in goal-directed navigation (e.g. reviewed in Burgess et al., 2002).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Bush et al., 2015 and Burgess et al., 2002.

claims.claim: Not all memories for items requires reconstruction of a spatial scene.
claims.source: However, not all memories for items requires reconstruction of a spatial scene.
claims.evidence: This is a limitation of the model's scope.

claims.claim: Recall of factual information (semantic memory) is not modeled.
claims.source: Recall of factual information (semantic memory) is not modeled, while memory for the attributes of an object irrespective of its context would require only perirhinal involvement.
claims.evidence: This is a limitation of the model's scope.

claims.claim: The BB-model only applies to imagery for coherent spatial scenes.
claims.source: The BB-model only applies to imagery for coherent spatial scenes, and suggests that this is necessary for episodic recollection in which the past event is 're-experienced' (Tulving, 1983), and certainly for remembering the spatial context of encountering an object.
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by citation to Tulving, 1983.

claims.claim: By informing perception in a top-down manner, the MTL can effectively predict perceptual input in familiar environments.
claims.source: By informing perception in a top-down manner, the MTL can effectively predict perceptual input in familiar environments, allowing novelty detection and enhancing perception with remembered information.
claims.evidence: This is a theoretical claim about the function of top-down connections.

claims.claim: If we view imagery as a top-down reconstruction of perceptual representations, the MTL together with the retrosplenial transformation circuit could be seen as a generative model for scenes.
claims.source: If we view imagery as a top-down reconstruction of perceptual representations, the MTL together with the retrosplenial transformation circuit could be seen as a generative model for scenes, consistent with generative models of memory such as (Káli and Dayan, 2001).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by citation to Káli and Dayan, 2001.

claims.claim: It has been proposed that the bottom-up/top-down transition between encoding and retrieving occurs rhythmically at the frequency of the theta rhythm.
claims.source: It has been proposed that the bottom-up/top-down transition between encoding and retrieving occurs rhythmically at the frequency of the theta rhythm (Hasselmo et al., 1996; Burgess et al., 2001a; Hasselmo et al., 2002; Byrne et al., 2007; Douchamps et al., 2013).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Hasselmo et al., 1996; Burgess et al., 2001a; Hasselmo et al., 2002; Byrne et al., 2007; Douchamps et al., 2013.

claims.claim: Theta might underlie a periodic probing of memorized representations.
claims.source: Theta might underlie a periodic probing of memorized representations; however, full recollection in imagery can last for long periods of time and need not correspond to specific phases of theta in humans (Düzel et al., 2010).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by citation to Düzel et al., 2010.

claims.claim: The relative strength of top-down and bottom-up connections can change smoothly and under control of the agent to allow memory representations to influence neural activity during perception.
claims.source: We have proposed (Figure 10) that the relative strength of top-down and bottom-up connections can change smoothly and under control of the agent (e.g. via the release of a neuromodulator) to allow memory representations to influence neural activity during perception.
claims.evidence: This is a theoretical claim of the model, with reference to Figure 10.

claims.claim: Tsao et al. (2013) recently reported 'trace cells' in lateral entorhinal cortex.
claims.source: Interestingly, Tsao et al. (2013) recently reported 'trace cells' in lateral entorhinal cortex, whose firing reflects the previous presence of a now missing object, while related 'mis-place' cells have been reported in CA1 (O'Keefe, 1976).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by citation to Tsao et al. (2013).

claims.claim: The trace cells of Tsao et al. (2013) do not fire when the object is present, but only in the subsequent absence of the object.
claims.source: However, the trace cells of Tsao et al. (2013) do not fire when the object is present, but only in the subsequent absence of the object. Thus they might signal the mismatch between the remembered object and its absence, that is reflecting a comparison of perceptually driven and memory driven firing of the model perirhinal cells.
claims.evidence: This is an interpretation of the experimental findings from Tsao et al. (2013).

claims.claim: Attentional modulation in the present model is crucial for unambiguous representations of multiple objects within a scene.
claims.source: Although we do not model the mechanistic origins of attention (see e.g. Itti and Koch, 2001), attentional modulation in the present model is crucial for unambiguous representations of multiple objects within a scene.
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by citation to Itti and Koch, 2001.

claims.claim: Objects must be sampled rhythmically and encoded sequentially in the parietal window.
claims.source: Thus, we require the objects to be sampled rhythmically and encoded sequentially in the parietal window (Figures 3 and 11), consistent with experimental literature suggesting rhythmic and sequential sampling (VanRullen et al., 2007; Landau and Fries, 2012; for review see VanRullen, 2013).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by citations to VanRullen et al., 2007; Landau and Fries, 2012; VanRullen, 2013, and reference to Figures 3 and 11.

claims.claim: If attentional cycles have a limited duration, there may be insufficient time for activity to build up if there are too many objects within a scene, producing a capacity limit.
claims.source: If attentional cycles have a limited duration, then there may be insufficient time for activity to build up in the corresponding neuronal populations and support robust encoding into memory if there are too many objects within a scene, producing a capacity limit (see also Lisman and Idiart, 1995; Bays and Husain, 2008).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Lisman and Idiart, 1995; Bays and Husain, 2008.

claims.claim: The proposed binding of OVCs and PRo neurons, subject to attention, might provide a functional interpretation of the hippocampus' role in memory-guided attention.
claims.source: The proposed binding of OVCs and PRo neurons, subject to attention, might also provide a functional interpretation of the hippocampus' role in memory-guided attention (e.g., Summerfield et al., 2006).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by citation to Summerfield et al., 2006.

claims.claim: The model suggests a role for grid cell activity in human spatial cognition.
claims.source: The model suggests a role for grid cell activity in human spatial cognition.
claims.evidence: This is a core claim of the model.

claims.claim: Humans likely make use of spatial imagery even in apparently non-visual tasks such as triangle completion in darkness.
claims.source: Indeed, humans likely make use of spatial imagery even in apparently non-visual tasks such as triangle completion in darkness (Tcheang et al., 2011), and there is evidence for grid-like brain activity during mental navigation (Bellmund et al., 2016; Horner et al. 2016).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Tcheang et al., 2011; Bellmund et al., 2016; Horner et al. 2016.

claims.claim: The model of mental navigation provides a mechanistic neural-level account of some aspects of 'scene construction' and 'episodic future thinking' with regard to familiar spaces.
claims.source: The model of mental navigation provides a mechanistic neural-level account of some aspects of 'scene construction' and 'episodic future thinking' (Schacter et al., 2007; Hassabis et al., 2007; Buckner, 2010) with regard to familiar spaces.
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Schacter et al., 2007; Hassabis et al., 2007; Buckner, 2010.

claims.claim: Mental navigation allows an agent to test future behavior, like the approach of a target from a new direction.
claims.source: Mental navigation allows an agent to test future behavior, like the approach of a target from a new direction as depicted in Video 12.
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by reference to Video 12.

claims.claim: The same neural infrastructure involved in scene perception and reconstruction also subserves planning and hypothesis testing.
claims.source: This suggests that the same neural infrastructure involved in scene perception and reconstruction also subserves planning and hypothesis testing (e.g. asking 'Which way should I go?' or 'What would I encounter if I went that way?').
claims.evidence: This is a theoretical claim about the function of the neural infrastructure.

claims.claim: The model suggests that sweeps of activity in the grid cell population may play a role in replay, forward sweeps, and could correspond to route planning.
claims.source: Nevertheless, the model suggests that sweeps of activity in the grid cell population may play are role in these aspects of place cell firing, and could correspond to route planning (Kubie and Fenton, 2012; Erdem and Hasselmo, 2012; Bush et al., 2015; Yamamoto and Tonegawa, 2017).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Kubie and Fenton, 2012; Erdem and Hasselmo, 2012; Bush et al., 2015; Yamamoto and Tonegawa, 2017.

results.result: The BB-model presents a systems-level computational framework integrating egocentric parietal representations with allocentric medial temporal lobe representations via a retrosplenial transformation circuit modulated by head direction cells. The model predicts novel cell types (egocentric and head-direction-modulated boundary- and object-vector cells) and explains how these populations interact to support spatial memory, scene construction, novelty detection, trace cells, and mental navigation.
results.evaluation: Claims C1-C3, C10-C12, C21-C31, and C82-C85 collectively describe the core architecture and theoretical contribution of the model. The model is explicitly described as extending prior work (C10), implementing bidirectional transformations between reference frames (C11-C12, C21-C26), and predicting new cell types (C2, C27-C30). The theoretical framework is well-articulated and internally consistent, spanning multiple levels of analysis (C83-C85). While this is a computational model rather than experimental validation, the theoretical claims are clearly stated and logically coherent.

results.result: The model proposes object vector cells (OVCs) as allocentric representations of object locations that allow items to be remembered within spatial contexts defined by environmental boundaries. These predicted OVCs map onto recently discovered neuronal populations and are consistent with experimental findings on object-location binding.
results.evaluation: Claims C4, C27-C28, and C54 describe the OVC prediction, which is supported by citations to recent experimental discoveries (Deshmukh and Knierim, 2013; Hoydal et al., 2017). Claims C86-C88 provide additional experimental support from human neuropsychology studies. The convergence between model predictions and experimental observations strengthens this result, though the model's OVCs are theoretical constructs that await direct experimental validation of all predicted properties.

results.result: Grid cells in the model update viewpoint during mental navigation and planning by driving sequential place cell activity, supporting shortcutting across unexplored terrain and generating preplay-like activity patterns. This mechanism provides a neural-level account of scene construction and episodic future thinking.
results.evaluation: Claims C5, C31, C46-C49, and C74-C78 describe the grid cell mechanism and its role in mental navigation. Claims C109-C114 extend this to human cognition. The model's grid cell implementation is supported by extensive citations to experimental literature (C46, C74-C76, C78) and recent human neuroimaging evidence (C75, C110). The simulation results (Figure 12-13, Videos 12-13) demonstrate the proposed mechanism. However, the model acknowledges limitations in capturing faster timescales of replay/preplay (C78), indicating incomplete coverage of the phenomenon.

results.result: Simulated lesions to Papez' circuit (removing head direction input) produce anterograde and retrograde amnesia by preventing the transformation between egocentric and allocentric representations, consistent with clinical observations of amnesia following lesions to the fornix and mammillary bodies.
results.evaluation: Claims C56-C60 describe the lesion simulation and its effects. The simulation results (Figure 7, Videos 5-6) demonstrate the predicted deficits. The model's predictions align with well-established clinical findings (C56-C57, supported by multiple citations). The mechanistic explanation—that head direction cells are necessary for the coordinate transformation—is internally consistent with the model architecture. However, real lesions affect multiple systems beyond head direction cells, so the model captures only one aspect of the clinical syndrome.

results.result: The model successfully simulates object novelty detection tasks, showing that an intact hippocampus generates mismatch signals when objects are moved or presented in different contexts, while hippocampal lesions abolish this discrimination. The model is robust to firing rate noise up to 20% and maintains performance with up to 20% neuron loss.
results.evaluation: Claims C61-C67 describe novelty detection simulations and robustness testing. The simulation results (Figures 8-9, Videos 7-8) demonstrate the predicted effects. The model's behavior matches experimental findings from rodent studies (C63, C66, C67, supported by citations to Mumby et al., 2002; Eacott and Norman, 2004; Langston and Wood, 2010). The robustness analysis (C61, Figure 8B-C) shows the model maintains high correlations between encoding and recall patterns despite perturbations. The quantitative correlation measures provide objective assessment of model performance.

results.result: The model proposes that periodic modulation of top-down connectivity (potentially corresponding to theta rhythm) allows comparison between perceived and remembered representations, generating 'trace' responses for missing objects or boundaries. Nominally non-spatial perirhinal neurons can exhibit spatial trace firing fields when reactivated at encoding locations.
results.evaluation: Claims C68-C71 and C102-C104 describe the trace cell mechanism. The simulation results (Figure 10, Videos 9-10) demonstrate trace responses in BVCs, OVCs, and perirhinal neurons. The model's predictions are compared to experimental findings (C70, C103, citing Tsao et al., 2013; O'Keefe, 1976). However, C104 notes a discrepancy: experimental trace cells fire only when objects are absent, while the model's mechanism differs. This suggests the model captures some but not all aspects of trace cell phenomena.

results.result: The model implements sequential attention to objects during encoding to solve the binding problem, ensuring unique associations between object identities and locations. This attentional mechanism is crucial for unambiguous representations and may explain capacity limits in visual working memory.
results.evaluation: Claims C42-C45 and C105-C108 describe the attention mechanism and its necessity. The theoretical argument for why attention is needed (C42-C43) is logically sound—without sequential sampling, multiple object-location conjunctions would be ambiguous. The implementation uses a fixed 600-time-unit cycle (C45), which is somewhat arbitrary but reasonable. Claims C106-C107 connect this to experimental literature on rhythmic sampling (VanRullen et al., 2007; Landau and Fries, 2012) and capacity limits (Lisman and Idiart, 1995; Bays and Husain, 2008). However, the attention mechanism is heuristically implemented rather than mechanistically modeled (C105), representing a limitation.

results.result: The model demonstrates that agents can sample multiple objects in imagery by shifting attention within the parietal window, allowing retrieval of object identities at different locations without changing the imagined viewpoint.
results.evaluation: Claims C72-C73 describe a well-known cognitive capability. The simulation (Figure 11, Video 11) demonstrates the mechanism: residual activity in the parietal window for non-cued objects can be boosted by attention, driving corresponding OVCs and ultimately retrieving object identity via learned OVC-to-perirhinal connections. This provides a mechanistic account of a known phenomenon, though the simulation is relatively simple (only 2 objects) and the attention mechanism remains heuristic.

results.result: The model implements head direction cells as a ring attractor updated by angular velocity, and uses a 20-sublayer retrosplenial transformation circuit with directionally-modulated boundary vector cells. Connection strengths are modulated by neuromodulation to switch between bottom-up (perception) and top-down (imagery) modes.
results.evaluation: Claims C33-C41 and C50 describe specific architectural and implementation details. The head direction ring attractor (C33-C34) is a standard model supported by citations (Skaggs et al., 1995; Zhang, 1996). The transformation circuit architecture (C35-C38) is clearly specified with 20 sublayers and reciprocal connections. The neuromodulatory switching mechanism (C39-C41) is supported by citation to Hasselmo, 2006, and implements a 95% reduction in non-active pathways. The Hebbian learning for grid-to-place connections (C50) is straightforward. These implementation details are internally consistent and well-documented.

results.result: The model incorporates established cell types (place cells, head direction cells, boundary vector cells, grid cells) with known firing properties and anatomical locations, and proposes that egocentric parietal representations interface with these allocentric MTL representations during scene construction tasks that engage the full network in humans.
results.evaluation: Claims C13-C20 and C32 describe well-established cell types with extensive experimental support (multiple citations for each). Claims C51-C52 describe the network engagement during scene construction, supported by numerous human neuroimaging studies. Claim C53 notes that BVCs were predicted by earlier versions of this model (Hartley et al., 2000; Burgess et al., 2001a), establishing precedent. Claim C55 documents the anatomical connectivity between proposed brain regions. These claims provide the empirical foundation for the model and are well-supported by the literature.

results.result: Scene construction and episodic future thinking depend on the hippocampal system, and episodic recollection requires reconstruction of viewpoint-specific representations, placing strong spatial constraints on how episodic memory works.
results.evaluation: Claims C6-C9 and C79-C81 establish the empirical and theoretical context for the model. These claims are supported by extensive citations to the scene construction and episodic memory literature (Tulving, 1985; Schacter et al., 2007; Hassabis et al., 2007; Buckner, 2010; O'Keefe and Nadel, 1978; etc.). The theoretical argument in C80-C81—that episodic re-experiencing requires viewpoint consistency—is conceptually sound and motivates the model's architecture. These are primarily contextual claims that frame the model's contribution rather than novel findings.

results.result: The model explains why place cells in open environments can associate with boundaries in all directions, why permanent landmarks evoke stronger retrosplenial responses, why head direction specifies viewing direction rather than movement direction, and how the encoding strategy supports object-cued recall and goal-directed navigation.
results.evaluation: Claims C89-C94 describe various explanatory capabilities of the model. Each claim provides a mechanistic account of known phenomena: direction-independent place cell firing (C89), landmark permanence effects (C90, citing Auger et al., 2012), head direction function (C91, citing Raudies et al., 2015; Maurer et al., 2014; Cei et al., 2014), recall mechanisms (C92), neural activity during imagery (C93, citing Burgess et al., 2001a; Hassabis et al., 2007; Schacter et al., 2007), and goal-directed navigation (C94, citing Bush et al., 2015; Burgess et al., 2002). These are theoretical explanations consistent with the model architecture and supported by relevant literature.

results.result: The model has explicit scope limitations: it does not address semantic memory, non-spatial item memory, or completely fictional scenes. It applies specifically to imagery for coherent spatial scenes necessary for episodic recollection. The model can be viewed as a generative model for scenes that predicts perceptual input and detects novelty.
results.evaluation: Claims C95-C97 explicitly acknowledge the model's limitations, which is appropriate for a computational model with specific scope. Claims C98-C99 describe the model's function as a generative/predictive system, supported by citation to Káli and Dayan, 2001. Claims C100-C101 discuss theta rhythm modulation, supported by multiple citations (Hasselmo et al., 1996; Burgess et al., 2001a; Hasselmo et al., 2002; Byrne et al., 2007; Douchamps et al., 2013; Düzel et al., 2010). These claims appropriately contextualize the model's scope and relate it to broader theoretical frameworks.
